title: CVIP Trieste | Owner's CAS/CAP for SIOT Tankers and Ro-Ro
description: CVIP at Trieste: an owner's CAS/CAP-style programme for crude tankers at SIOT and Turkish-trade ro-ro ships, built from short calls into one trend record.
h1: Comprehensive Vessel Inspection Programme at Trieste: an owner's condition assessment for SIOT crude tankers and the ro-ro freighters on Turkish trailer runs
intro: Trieste sees two kinds of ship again and again: crude tankers pumping cargo ashore at the SIOT terminal for the Transalpine Pipeline, and ro-ro freighters shuttling trailers to and from Turkey. Neither stays long, which is exactly why CVIP, our Comprehensive Vessel Inspection Programme, suits them. In the owner's language it is an owner's CAS or owner's CAP, meaning a survey of the entire ship built the way those schemes are built, but ordered by the owner for the owner's purposes rather than by class. A baseline visit and later visits on regular Trieste calls build one trend record, and our technicians fly in from India for each of them.

highlights.h: Discharge windows that come round again
highlights.p: A crude tanker supplying the Transalpine Pipeline returns to the Bay of Muggia on a pattern the charterer can usually predict. Each discharge gives a fixed spell for deck, piping, forecastle spaces and cargo pumps under load, so the programme books its tanker modules against calls already planned.

highlights.h: Two ends of one ro-ro rotation
highlights.p: Some trailer ships on the Turkish runs shuttle between Trieste and Pendik on Istanbul's Anatolian shore. Vehicle decks, ramps and ballast tanks can then be divided between the two terminals, so the whole-ship assessment advances at both ends of the route without a lost sailing.

highlights.h: The yard leg across the Adriatic
highlights.p: Cargo tanks are seldom gas-free at an oil terminal, so a tanker's tank round waits for the yard. When the ship heads for a northern Adriatic repair yard such as Viktor Lenac near Rijeka, the same team and point numbering follow her, and the dock visit slots into the record.

sections.h: Where in the Trieste port system an owner's condition assessment takes place
p: Trieste offers no lay-by berth where a tanker or ro-ro ship sits idle for days, so a programme here is assembled from working calls, anchorage waits and a yard stay elsewhere in the northern Adriatic. Each place contributes the modules its conditions allow, and the programme plan records which module belongs to which place before the baseline is booked.

Terminal rules shape what is possible as much as time does. At SIOT the terminal's own safety regime decides which instruments may come aboard and who may walk the jetty, so the agent obtains clearance and the induction before each visit, and the work plan states which readings are taken from the deck and which wait for a gas-free ship.
list: SIOT jetties in the Bay of Muggia: main deck plating, deck lines and manifolds, forecastle spaces, ballast tanks the master declares safe, and cargo pump drives read while discharge runs
Ro-ro berths of the port: vehicle decks, internal and stern ramps, lashing points and the ballast tanks below the main deck, one block per call
Trieste Marine Terminal on Molo VII: hatch covers, cross-deck structure and scrubber overboard lines on container ships during cargo work
Anchorage in the Gulf of Trieste: machinery and deck modules by launch while a ship waits for SIOT or a berth
Monfalcone commercial quays: hold frames and hatch coamings on bulk carriers once their holds are empty
Northern Adriatic repair yards, Viktor Lenac near Rijeka among them: cargo tanks, the dry bottom and sea chests when the tanker docks

sections.h: Crude tankers at SIOT: a programme built around vetting and the CAP decision
p: The tankers that feed the pipeline to Austria, southern Germany and the Czech Republic are looked at by oil-major vetting departments every time they are fixed. As a tanker ages, the questions shift from paperwork to steel: what state are the ballast tanks in, how fast is under-deck structure wasting, and will the ship earn the CAP rating a charterer may ask for. A single survey answers those questions once. A programme that visits on successive Trieste discharges shows whether the answers are getting better or worse.

That trend is what a technical manager needs when choosing between three courses: book a class CAP survey now, carry out steel renewal at the next docking and book CAP afterwards, or sell the ship before either. Ballast tank coating ratings photographed from the same viewpoint each call, deck readings at numbered points, and cargo pump vibration taken during comparable discharges give that choice a measured basis.

Cargo tanks are the gap at a terminal. They are examined and gauged when the ship is gas-freed at a yard, and the programme treats that docking as its main checkpoint: a pre-docking round on an earlier Trieste call sets the expected renewal list, and the dock visit confirms or corrects it.

sections.h: Turkish-trade ro-ro ships: spreading a whole-ship assessment across a rotation
p: Trailer traffic is hard on a ro-ro ship. Vehicle decks wear and dish where trailers turn, lashing pockets crack and corrode, ramp hinges and their seals take punishment at every berth, and the ballast tanks below the main deck suffer from condensation and from salt carried aboard on the trailers themselves. A ship that arrives and sails within the same day cannot be opened up in one call, but one that keeps returning can be assessed a block at a time.

In the programme plan the ship is divided into blocks: a group of vehicle deck strakes, one ramp and its hinges, a pair of ballast tanks, the engine room. Each Trieste call takes the next block, and where the rotation also calls at Pendik, some blocks can be taken at the Turkish end, subject to the team holding Turkish visas. After a set number of calls the whole ship has been covered once, which forms the baseline, and the cycle repeats so each block collects its second, third and fourth set of readings.

Machinery suits the same rhythm. Ramp hydraulic power packs, ventilation fans for the cargo decks and the main switchboards are read during cargo work, when they actually run, so vibration and thermal trends are built under the load the ship works at every week rather than on a quiet day alongside.

sections.h: Owner's CAS and owner's CAP for a Trieste caller: what the programme borrows, and what it cannot award
p: A request for an owner's CAP on a tanker discharging at SIOT, or an owner's CAS on an older ro-ro freighter, is a request for the discipline of those schemes without their paperwork. CVIP keeps the discipline: a survey plan drawn from the ship's drawings and survey history, close-up examination to that plan, thickness at defined positions, coating condition in GOOD, FAIR and POOR terms, machinery assessed under load, and graded findings collected in one report on the whole ship.

It cannot award what the official schemes award. The IMO Condition Assessment Scheme, which concerns a narrow group of older tankers, closes with the flag Administration issuing a Statement of Compliance; the Condition Assessment Programme ends in a rating issued by the ship's classification society. Neither comes out of CVIP. If a vetting department insists on a class CAP rating, that survey is arranged with the society, usually during a yard stay, and the programme's readings indicate beforehand where the ship is likely to stand.

Thickness readings follow the same line. A class survey accepts gauging solely from firms holding the ship's society's approval under IACS UR Z17. Atlantis is still going through that approval process with DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS, and no certificate has been issued yet. CVIP readings at Trieste therefore serve the owner's own decisions on steel, docking, chartering and sale, and are not offered for class credit.

sections.h: Planning visits around terminal clearance, Schengen visas and the run to the yard
p: Tanker and ro-ro calls at Trieste are often confirmed close to the date, which is awkward for a team that needs Schengen visas issued in India. A programme removes most of that difficulty, because it is planned against the ship's expected calls over months rather than one nominated arrival. We ask the operator for the rotation or the trading pattern, the next docking and the class survey dates, and each technician's visa is applied for to cover a run of calls rather than a single one.

For the baseline we need structural drawings with original scantlings, the latest thickness measurement report, the class survey status with any outstanding items, the machinery register held in the planned maintenance system, and whatever vibration or thermal surveys have been done before. The ship provides permits and gas-free certificates for spaces to be entered, and an engineer who can bring each machine to the load agreed in the plan. The agent handles ISPS access at the ro-ro and container berths, SIOT clearance and launches for the Gulf anchorage. The team usually flies into Trieste Airport at Ronchi dei Legionari, which also puts Monfalcone within easy reach. Programme questions for Trieste can be sent to info@atlantisndt.com, or through the enquiry form further down.

faqs.q: Is CVIP at Trieste the same as CAS or CAP?
faqs.a: Not in standing. The working method is close enough that owners borrow the names, but the owner orders the programme and receives every report. Nothing goes to a flag Administration for review and no society grades the ship from it, so it ends without a Statement of Compliance or a CAP rating. A charterer who insists on the class CAP gets it from the society; the programme tells the owner the probable result in advance.

faqs.q: Can a SIOT tanker's cargo tanks be included in the programme?
faqs.a: Yes, but not at the terminal. Cargo tanks need the ship gas-freed and certified for entry, which does not happen during discharge at SIOT. At Trieste the programme covers deck, deck lines, forecastle spaces, safe ballast tanks and cargo pumps under load; the cargo tank round is planned for the next yard stay, often in the northern Adriatic, with the same team and the same numbered points.

faqs.q: Can programme visits on a ro-ro ship be split between Trieste and Pendik?
faqs.a: Where the ship's rotation calls at both, yes. The block plan is the same at either end, so a ramp examined at Trieste and a group of vehicle deck strakes gauged at Pendik land in one record. Pendik visits need Turkish visas in addition to the Schengen visas that Trieste requires, so we plan the two sets of applications together against the rotation.

faqs.q: Does the Mediterranean ECA change what the programme watches on Trieste ro-ro and container ships?
faqs.a: It raises the priority of scrubber piping. Since May 2025 the Adriatic has been inside the Mediterranean SOx ECA, so scrubber-fitted ships run their systems for the whole passage to Trieste. Wash-water and overboard lines, discharge valves and the shell around outlets are gauged at fixed points on each visit, and the trend shows how fast they are thinning before a leak forces the decision.

faqs.q: Can bulk carriers at Monfalcone join a Trieste fleet programme?
faqs.a: Yes. Monfalcone sits in the same port system, a short drive from Trieste, so a bulk carrier discharging there can be visited on the same mobilisation as a tanker at SIOT or a ro-ro ship in Trieste. Holds are measured once empty, with access agreed with the stevedores, and the bulk carrier keeps its own report and trend record within the fleet programme.

faqs.q: What does a charterer or lender see from a Trieste programme?
faqs.a: A measured history rather than a snapshot. After a few visits the owner can show coating ratings for each ballast tank over time, corrosion rates at numbered points, crack findings and their repair, and machinery trends for cargo pumps or ramp hydraulics. The owner decides who receives it; the record and the data files stay with the owner and can pass to a buyer if the ship is sold.
